report.headline: EuroLeague high-usage playmaker projected to shrink to near-average NBA usage; shooting-efficiency projection carries no signal

projection.text: Player A is projected to use 19.5% of NBA possessions, down from 24.7% in the 2012-13 EuroLeague season and just below the league-average usage of 20.1%; the 80% interval (14.6%–24.3%) spans roughly two standard deviations of NBA usage (SD 4.8%), so the model can rank but not pin down an individual value.

risks.text: A 17.3% turnover rate in the source season is elevated for a high-usage ball-handler.

Projected NBA usage of 19.5% falls well short of the 25.1% the z-preservation baseline implies if Player A held exactly their EuroLeague standing, reflecting the typical role compression that comes with this move.

For what it's worth, the true shooting projection sits below both the NBA average (54.1%) and the z-preservation baseline (54.4%), hinting at downside on efficiency, though this metric's model underperforms a trivial baseline and should be discounted.
The estimate rests on only 61 historical EL->NBA transitions, a modest sample for a move of this kind.

strengths.text: In the source season Player A posted a 25.8% assist rate and 4.693 assists per 75 possessions, indicating a significant playmaking role.
Player A's usage rate sat 1.04 standard deviations above the EuroLeague average, reflecting a heavy offensive workload before the move.
Shooting efficiency in the EuroLeague was solid at 56.5% true shooting, essentially at league average (+0.06 sd).
A three-point rate of 38.1% of shot attempts in the EuroLeague points to a floor-spacing shot profile.

uncertainty.text: The true shooting projection (52.5%, 80% interval 46.6%–58.5%) should not be treated as informative: its out-of-fold error (4.7%) is no better than a naive league-average baseline, meaning the model adds nothing beyond guessing the mean for this metric.
